title: John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
summary: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness of Judea, dressed like Elijah, calling people to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near and baptizing them in the Jordan. He warns the Pharisees and Sadducees that descent from Abraham will not save them and announces a coming one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Jesus comes to be baptized, and as he rises from the water the Spirit descends on him like a dove and the Father's voice declares him his beloved Son.
story:
Nearly three decades pass between chapters 2 and 3 (Luke 3:23 says Jesus was about thirty when he began his ministry), and Matthew bridges them with the vague “In those days”. He moves straight from the child in Nazareth to the grown man, and he introduces him through John, the forerunner Malachi had promised: “Behold, I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me” (Malachi 3:1), and “I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). Jesus later says plainly that John “is the Elijah who was to come” (11:14).

John's message of repentance and coming judgment picks up where the prophets left off, and his location, in the wilderness by the Jordan, recalls the place where Israel once waited to cross into the promised land. The chapter continues the pattern of chapter 2, in which Jesus relives Israel's story. Having been called out of Egypt as God's son (2:15), he now passes through the waters, as Israel passed through the sea and the Jordan, and is declared God's beloved Son. The next chapter will take him, like Israel, into the wilderness to be tested. John's message in verse 2 is also exactly the message Jesus will preach in 4:17, so that the forerunner's preaching becomes the Messiah's.
historical:
John the Baptist was a well-known prophetic figure in his own right. Josephus (Antiquities 18.116-119, written around AD 93 to 94) calls him a good man who urged the Jews to practice virtue, justice toward one another, and piety toward God, and so to come to baptism, which Josephus understood as a purification of the body for those whose souls had already been cleansed by righteousness. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, feared his influence over the crowds and had him executed at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Luke dates the start of John's preaching to the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius (Luke 3:1), which is AD 28 or 29 if counted from Augustus's death in AD 14, or a year or two earlier if counted from Tiberius's shared rule with Augustus. The traditional site of Jesus' baptism lies near Jericho, on the east bank at Al-Maghtas (Bethany beyond the Jordan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015) and on the west bank at Qasr al-Yahud.

The Judean wilderness, the dry hill country falling from Jerusalem to the Dead Sea, was a place of refuge and of hope. Isaiah 40:3 had pictured a road prepared in the wilderness for God's return, and the community whose library was found at Qumran, a few miles south of the Jordan's mouth, applied that verse to itself: the Community Rule (1QS 8:13-16) explains its withdrawal to the desert as preparing the way of the Lord by the study of the Law. The same scroll insists that washing cannot cleanse anyone who refuses God's discipline (1QS 3:4-9) and looks for a day when God will cleanse his people with a holy spirit, sprinkling a spirit of truth on them like waters of purification (1QS 4:20-21). The parallels with John are close: the wilderness, Isaiah 40:3, washing joined to repentance, and a coming cleansing by the Spirit. John A. T. Robinson (Harvard Theological Review, 1957) proposed that John had been raised among such a community, noting Luke 1:80, which says he lived in the wilderness until his public appearance. Others, such as Joan Taylor (The Immerser, 1997), find no evidence that John belonged to any sect, and note the differences: Qumran's washings were repeated, private, and limited to members who had passed a long probation, while John's baptism was once for all, public, and offered to all Israel. Josephus's own youthful teacher, a desert ascetic named Bannus who wore clothing from trees, ate what grew wild, and bathed often for purity (Life 11-12), shows that John was not the only such figure.

The Pharisees and Sadducees were two of the main parties of the day. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to exact observance of the law of Moses together with the traditions of the elders, and they had wide influence among ordinary people (Josephus, Antiquities 13.297-298, 18.12-15). The Sadducees came mostly from the priestly aristocracy connected with the temple; they rejected the Pharisees' traditions and denied the resurrection of the dead (Antiquities 18.16-17; Acts 23:8). The two parties often opposed each other, yet Matthew alone pairs them five times (3:7; 16:1, 6, 11, 12) as a single front. Luke's version of the same speech is addressed to the crowds (Luke 3:7). Matthew's pairing makes John's warning fall on the religious leadership as a whole.
cultural:
Washing with water was part of ordinary Jewish life. The law required ritual washings to remove impurity (Leviticus 15), and archaeologists have found hundreds of stepped immersion pools (mikvaot) from this period, in Jerusalem, at Qumran, at Sepphoris, and at Masada; the Mishnah later devoted a whole tractate (Mikvaot) to them. John's baptism was different in several ways. It was administered by John rather than self-immersion, it was given once, it was joined to confession of sins, and it prepared people for the coming judgment and the one who would follow him. Whether Jews already immersed Gentile converts at this date is debated. The Mishnah (Pesahim 8:8) records the schools of Shammai and Hillel, both early first century, disputing when a new convert may immerse and eat the Passover, which suggests the practice was known; but the fuller rabbinic rules (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 46a-47b) are later. If proselyte immersion was practiced, John's demand that Jews themselves be washed as though they were outsiders would have been all the more shocking.

John's clothing, “a garment of camel's hair, with a leather belt around his waist” (verse 4), deliberately recalls Elijah, of whom the king's messengers said, “He was a hairy man,” “with a leather belt around his waist” (2 Kings 1:8), and the hairy mantle was a prophet's dress (Zechariah 13:4). Locusts were a permitted food (Leviticus 11:22), and the Damascus Document (CD 12:14-15) prescribes how to cook them, roasted or boiled. A Jewish-Christian gospel used by the Ebionites, quoted by Epiphanius (Panarion 30.13.4-5), changed John's locusts (akrides) to honey cakes (enkrides) to make him vegetarian. Wild honey could be bees' honey from the rocks (Deuteronomy 32:13) or sweet sap from trees. This was the food of a man living on what the land gave.

John's images come from farm and field. Vipers fleeing a brush fire give his opening insult its force: the leaders are running from the coming wrath like snakes before the flames. His words about stones and children may carry a Hebrew or Aramaic wordplay, since ʾeben (stone) and ben (son), or in Aramaic ʾabnayyā and bĕnayyā, sound alike. The axe at the root recalls Isaiah's picture of God felling the proud forest (Isaiah 10:33-34). Carrying sandals was a slave's task; a later rabbinic saying (Babylonian Talmud, Ketubbot 96a) holds that a disciple should do for his teacher every service a slave does except untying his sandal. The threshing floor was a flat, hard surface where harvested grain was beaten and then tossed into the wind with a winnowing fork (ptuon), so that the heavy grain fell and the chaff blew aside to be burned; “unquenchable fire” echoes Isaiah 66:24. Finally, the voice from heaven would have reminded Jewish hearers of the bat qol, the daughter of a voice. The Tosefta (Sotah 13:2-3) says that after Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi died, the holy spirit departed from Israel, but a heavenly voice was still heard. Matthew's scene claims more: the heavens open, the Spirit comes, and God speaks of his Son.
literary:
The chapter has three scenes: John's preaching (verses 1 to 6), his warning to the religious leaders (verses 7 to 12), and Jesus' baptism (verses 13 to 17). Matthew introduces John with a formula like his fulfillment quotations, “This is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah” (verse 3), and quotes Isaiah 40:3 in the form found in the Septuagint and in Mark. In Hebrew, the parallel lines put the wilderness with the road (“Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness”); in the Greek, the phrase can go with the voice, a voice crying in the wilderness, which fits John's location. The Gospels also change Isaiah's “for our God” to “for Him”, so that the Lord whose way is prepared becomes Jesus.

John's warning (verses 7 to 12) is almost word for word the same as Luke 3:7-9 and 3:16-17, one of the clearest examples of material shared by Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark, which the Two-Source view assigns to the sayings source Q and the Farrer view explains by Luke's use of Matthew. The speech moves from accusation (verse 7) to demand (verse 8) to warning against false security (verse 9) to the imminence of judgment (verse 10), and then turns to the coming one, who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire and clear his threshing floor (verses 11 and 12). Its images, vipers, stones, an axe, a threshing floor, and fire, come from the prophets' language of judgment.

Verses 14 and 15, John's protest and Jesus' reply, are found only in Matthew, and they contain Jesus' first words in the Gospel: “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.” The two key words of the reply, fulfill and righteousness, become themes of the book (5:17, 5:20, 6:33). The scene closes with a revelation from heaven that combines echoes of Psalm 2:7, where God addresses his anointed king, “You are My Son”, Isaiah 42:1, where God speaks of his chosen servant in whom his soul delights and on whom he puts his Spirit, and perhaps Genesis 22:2, where Isaac is Abraham's beloved only son. Matthew's form, “This is My beloved Son” (third person), makes the voice a public announcement, where Mark and Luke have “You are My beloved Son”. The same words return at the transfiguration (17:5). The chapter also forms the first half of a frame around the Gospel: Father, Son, and Spirit appear together here at the beginning of Jesus' ministry, and the one name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit appears in the baptismal command at the end (28:19).

outline.t: John preaches repentance in the wilderness
Warning to the Pharisees and Sadducees
The coming one who baptizes with the Spirit and fire
The Spirit descends and the Father speaks

doctrines.note: John's first word is “Repent”, and he commands, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance” (verse 8), a changed life and not merely a ritual or a pedigree. People confess their sins as they are baptized (verse 6). Repentance is urgent because God's reign is near, and in Matthew it is the first word of both John and Jesus (3:2, 4:17).

The kingdom of heaven is God's reign breaking into history. Matthew prefers kingdom of heaven, following the Jewish reverence that avoided speaking God's name, but means the same as kingdom of God. John announces it as near, bringing both salvation for those who turn and judgment for those who do not.

John speaks of the coming wrath, the axe at the root, and the chaff burned with unquenchable fire (verses 7, 10, and 12). The coming one both gathers and judges. Descent from Abraham gives no immunity; God looks for fruit. Matthew keeps this note of judgment throughout, to the sheep and the goats of chapter 25.

John's water baptism prepares for the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (verse 11), and Jesus' own baptism stands behind the baptism he later commands in the triune name (28:19). Christians differ on the mode and the subjects of baptism and on how John's baptism relates to Christian baptism, but nearly all practice it in obedience to Jesus' command.

At the baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit of God descends on him, and the Father speaks from heaven (verses 16 and 17). The church has long seen here one of the clearest revelations of the one God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three distinct persons acting together, a revelation completed in the single name of 28:19.

words.note: Metanoeō, to repent, change one's mind. It occurs 34 times in the New Testament, five in Matthew, and the noun metanoia (verses 8 and 11) another 22 times. BDAG gives its sense as to change one's mind and, in religious use, to turn about in one's thinking and conduct. Its Greek sense is a change of mind, but in the Gospels it carries the weight of the Hebrew prophets' call to turn back (shuv) to God with the whole life, which is why John demands fruit. Repentance is not a feeling alone, and it is not penance, as the Latin paenitentiam agite (do penance) was later read; Erasmus's notes to his Greek New Testament (first published 1516) pressed that point, and Luther built on it.

Basileia, kingdom, kingship, reign. It occurs about 162 times in the New Testament and 55 times in Matthew, more than in any other book. Matthew uses the phrase kingdom of heaven (literally of the heavens) 32 times and kingdom of God only four or five times; the phrase is unique to Matthew in the New Testament. It refers to God's rule more than to a place, and heaven stands reverently for God, as in the prodigal's I have sinned against heaven (Luke 15:18).

Baptizō, to dip, immerse, wash. It occurs about 77 times in the New Testament. In ordinary Greek it could mean to plunge or sink, and in Jewish Greek it was used of ritual washing (Mark 7:4, Luke 11:38). Christians disagree on whether baptism should be by immersion, pouring, or sprinkling, and on whether it is for believers only or also for their children; the word's range is broad enough that each tradition appeals to it, and none can settle the question from the verb alone.

Orgē, wrath, anger. It occurs 36 times in the New Testament, twelve in Romans, and only here in Matthew, in “the coming wrath” (verse 7; compare Luke 3:7 and 1 Thessalonians 1:10). BDAG describes it here as the future judgment of God. It is not a loss of temper but God's settled opposition to evil, which the prophets had announced for the day of the LORD (Zephaniah 1:15).

Dikaiosynē, righteousness, justice. It occurs about 92 times in the New Testament, 34 of them in Romans, and seven times in Matthew (3:15; 5:6, 10, 20; 6:1, 33; 21:32). In Matthew it usually means conduct that conforms to God's will, the right way of life that God requires; in 21:32 John himself came in the way of righteousness. When Jesus speaks of fulfilling all righteousness in verse 15 he means doing everything God requires, including identifying with the people he came to save; readers should not read Paul's meaning of the righteousness God gives into Matthew's use without care.

Peristera, dove, pigeon. It occurs ten times in the New Testament, in the baptism accounts of all four Gospels and in the doves sold in the temple (21:12). No Old Testament text calls the Spirit a dove, but readers have heard echoes of the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), which a rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 15a) compared to a dove hovering over her young, and of Noah's dove bringing news of a new world (Genesis 8:8-12). Matthew says the Spirit descended like a dove, describing the manner of its coming.

Agapētos, beloved, dear. It occurs about 61 times in the New Testament, often in the letters as a term of address (dear friends), and three times in Matthew (3:17, 12:18, 17:5). In the Greek Old Testament it translates yachid, only, for Isaac in Genesis 22:2, and so can carry the sense of an only and dearly loved son. The Father's word, My beloved Son, speaks of a unique relationship, not of approval earned.

Eudokeō, to be well pleased, to take delight, to choose. It occurs 21 times in the New Testament, three in Matthew (3:17, 12:18, 17:5). In Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1, it describes the servant in whom God's soul delights, which confirms that the voice at the baptism alludes to the servant songs. The aorist tense refers to the Father's delight without implying a moment when it began; Jesus has not yet preached or healed, and the Father's pleasure rests on who he is.

christ:
The baptism reveals who Jesus is and what he has come to do. The Father declares, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!” The words join the royal Son of Psalm 2, “You are My Son”, with the servant of Isaiah 42, “My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him”, the servant who will bring justice to the nations and who, later in Isaiah, will bear the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Jesus is both: the Messiah-King of David's line and the servant who suffers for his people. The echo of Isaac, Abraham's beloved son offered on the mountain (Genesis 22:2), may point in the same direction.

The Spirit comes upon him to equip him for his work, as Isaiah promised of the shoot from Jesse, “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him” (Isaiah 11:2), and of the anointed one who would preach good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1). The heavens are opened, as Isaiah had prayed, “If only You would rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). The one on whom the Spirit rests is also the one who will give the Spirit: John promises that he will baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire, the gift the prophets foresaw (Ezekiel 36:26-27; Joel 2:28) and that the risen Christ pours out at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:1-4).

John rightly sees that Jesus has nothing to confess and should be baptizing him. Yet Jesus insists on being baptized, standing with sinners in the water of repentance. Many interpreters see this as the first sign of his mission to take the place of his people, a mission completed at the cross, which Jesus himself calls a baptism: “But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50). The chapter also shows Jesus reliving Israel's story as the obedient Son. Israel passed through the waters and was tested in the wilderness; Jesus comes up out of the water and is declared the Son, and the next chapter leads him into the wilderness. The Son who fulfills all righteousness is the one who will fulfill the Law and the Prophets (5:17).
interpretation:
From the beginning the church asked why Jesus was baptized. Ignatius of Antioch knew Matthew's answer (To the Smyrnaeans 1.1: baptized by John so that all righteousness might be fulfilled by him) and gave his own: he was baptized so that by his suffering he might cleanse the water (To the Ephesians 18.2). A Jewish-Christian gospel that Jerome calls the Gospel according to the Hebrews (Against Pelagius 3.2) has Jesus' mother and brothers urge him to be baptized and Jesus ask what sin he had committed that he should go. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 88) reports that when Jesus went down into the water a fire was kindled in the Jordan, and the Old Latin Codex Vercellensis adds to Matthew that a great light shone from the water. Adoptionist teachers such as Theodotus of Byzantium in Rome around 190 held that the Spirit or the Christ came upon a mere man at the baptism, a view the church rejected (Hippolytus, Refutation 7.35; Eusebius, Church History 5.28).

In the East the baptism became the heart of the feast of Theophany on 6 January, celebrated with the Great Blessing of the Waters, and Gregory of Nazianzus preached his oration On the Holy Lights (Oration 39) at Constantinople for the feast in 381. The Roman calendar keeps the Baptism of the Lord on the Sunday after Epiphany. Thomas Aquinas devoted a question of the Summa Theologiae to it (III, question 39), arguing that Christ was baptized not to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters and give them power to sanctify. At the Reformation, Luther's baptismal rite (Taufbüchlein, 1523) included his Flood Prayer, which says that through the baptism of Christ in the Jordan God sanctified all water for a saving flood, and his hymn Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam (1541) became the basis of Bach's cantata BWV 7 for the feast of John the Baptist (24 June 1724). Calvin argued that John's baptism and the apostles' were in substance the same (Institutes 4.15.7-8), against the medieval teaching that John's was only preparatory. Anabaptists and later Baptists read the chapter's confession and repentance as marks of a believer's baptism; other traditions read the baptism of Jesus as God's claim on a person that precedes any response.

In art the scene appears in the fifth- and sixth-century mosaics of the Orthodox (Neonian) and Arian baptisteries in Ravenna, where the river Jordan is personified as an old man, in Piero della Francesca's Baptism of Christ (fifteenth century, National Gallery, London), and in the Baptism of Christ by Andrea del Verrocchio, on which the young Leonardo da Vinci painted an angel (Uffizi, Florence). Modern historians count the baptism among the most secure facts about Jesus, precisely because the early church found it awkward: John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volumes 1 and 2, 1991 and 1994) uses it as a chief example of the criterion of embarrassment. Joan Taylor's The Immerser (1997) set John in the world of Jewish purity practice, and the Dead Sea Scrolls, from 1947 on, renewed interest in John's wilderness setting.
text:
Several small differences appear between manuscripts and between English Bibles. In verse 6 the earliest manuscripts read ‘in the Jordan River’, while later ones, followed by the King James Version, read simply ‘in Jordan’. In verse 11 the words ‘and with fire’ are in the earliest manuscripts and in the King James Version but are missing from most late Byzantine manuscripts. In verse 16 the words ‘to him’ (the heavens were opened to him) are absent from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and from Codex Vaticanus, and some editions print them in brackets. In verse 17 Codex Bezae and some Syriac manuscripts read ‘You are my beloved Son’, bringing Matthew into line with Mark and Luke; the harder reading, ‘This is’, is almost certainly original. After verse 15 the Old Latin Codex Vercellensis and at least one other Old Latin manuscript add that a great light shone from the water when Jesus was baptized, so that all who were there were afraid.

The quotation of Isaiah 40:3 in verse 3 follows the Septuagint's wording, in which ‘in the wilderness’ can be taken with the voice; the Hebrew, as the BSB of Isaiah shows, joins it to the command to prepare the way.

teach.big: God's promised forerunner calls Israel to real repentance before the coming King, and Jesus, standing with sinners in the water, is revealed by the Father and anointed by the Spirit as the beloved Son.

outline.t: God's reign is near, so the first word of the gospel is repent: a turning of the whole life toward God.
John is the voice Isaiah promised and the Elijah Malachi foretold; his wilderness life and dress announce that the prophets' hope is being fulfilled.
Crowds from Jerusalem and Judea come out to confess their sins; renewal begins with honest confession.
Religious heritage and status give no protection from judgment; God looks for the fruit of a changed life.
John points away from himself to the stronger one who will baptize with the Spirit and fire, gathering his wheat and judging the chaff.
The sinless Son chooses to stand with sinners, fulfilling all righteousness by identifying with the people he came to save.
Heaven opens: the Spirit rests on Jesus and the Father names him beloved Son before he has done any public work.

teach.pitfalls:
Preachers often turn John into an angry street preacher and license harshness in his name. His severity is aimed at religious leaders who assumed they were safe, and his call is to fruit, not to anger. Do not use brood of vipers to insult present-day opponents or, worse, Jews; Matthew's target is presumption among the religious, which includes the church.

Other misreadings: arguing the mode of baptism from the verb baptizō or from the phrase went up out of the water, which describes leaving the river rather than the manner of baptism; teaching that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism, which contradicts chapters 1 and 2; treating the Spirit's descent as though the Spirit had never been with Jesus before (1:18, 20); and reading fulfill all righteousness as if Jesus needed to earn God's favor. The fire of verse 11 is read by some as the purifying fire of Pentecost and by others as the fire of judgment in verses 10 and 12; teach the question rather than hide it. Finally, avoid presenting the baptism only as a proof text for the Trinity. It is that, but it is first a scene of the Son's humility and the Father's delight.
teach.pastoral: John's call to repentance can press hard on tender consciences. People prone to scrupulosity may hear verses 10 to 12 as a threat they can never escape. Teach that repentance is a turning toward God, whose Son stands in the water with sinners, and that the Father's delight in verse 17 comes before any achievement. Those raised in church who have relied on family faith (We have Abraham as our father) need the warning, but those who are newcomers or ashamed of their past need to hear that crowds of ordinary sinners came and were received. People uncertain about the validity of their own baptism can be pointed to Christ's baptism as the ground of theirs.

hard.q: Why did Jesus, who had no sin, receive a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins?
hard.a:
The objection was felt from the first. A Jewish-Christian gospel quoted by Jerome (Against Pelagius 3.2) has Jesus ask what sin he had committed that he should be baptized, and Matthew himself records John's protest. Modern historians sharpen it. John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, 1991 and 1994) counts the baptism among the surest facts about Jesus precisely because it embarrassed the early church, and many critical scholars conclude that the historical Jesus began as a disciple of John, accepting his message of repentance and perhaps, like other Jews, confessing sins in his baptism; on this view Matthew's dialogue in verses 14 and 15 is a later explanation of an awkward fact. If Jesus underwent a baptism for sinners, the argument runs, he likely thought of himself as one of them.

Christian interpreters have answered in several complementary ways. Some emphasize identification: Jesus takes his place among sinners as their representative, as the servant of Isaiah 53:12 is “numbered with the transgressors”, and his baptism anticipates the death he calls a baptism (Luke 12:50). Others emphasize obedience: John's baptism was God's summons to Israel at that moment (21:25, 32), and Jesus submits to every part of God's will, which is what fulfill all righteousness means. Others see a public commissioning, the moment of his anointing with the Spirit (Acts 10:38). Justin Martyr (Dialogue 88) said Jesus did not need baptism but submitted for humanity's sake; Ignatius and Aquinas said he was baptized to cleanse the waters rather than to be cleansed by them. These readings do not compete. The New Testament states that Jesus was without sin (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22), and the historical argument cannot prove what Jesus thought of himself from the fact of his baptism alone; it remains a question on which historians and believers read the same evidence differently.

hard.q: Does the baptism show that Jesus became the Son of God only when the Spirit came on him?
hard.a:
The objection has ancient and modern defenders. In the late second century Theodotus of Byzantium taught at Rome that Jesus was a man born of a virgin on whom the Christ or the Spirit descended at the baptism, and the Ebionites held related views. Modern critics argue that the earliest Christian belief was that Jesus was exalted to divine sonship, at his resurrection (Romans 1:4) or at his baptism, and that Mark, which begins with the baptism and has the voice say “You are My beloved Son”, reflects that stage. Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) sets out this development, and some manuscripts of Luke 3:22 even read Psalm 2:7, ‘today I have begotten you’, at the baptism.

Matthew's own narrative answers the question differently. He has already told of Jesus' conception by the Holy Spirit (1:18, 20), his name Immanuel, God with us (1:23), and God's own words, ‘Out of Egypt I called My Son’ (2:15), before the baptism. His form of the voice, “This is My beloved Son”, is a declaration to others about what Jesus already is, not an act that makes him Son. Scholars such as Larry Hurtado (Lord Jesus Christ, 2003) and Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) argue that the earliest Christians already gave Jesus a place within the identity of Israel's God, so that a straight line from low to high views is too simple. The church rejected adoptionism and confesses in the Nicene Creed that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father. Within that confession, Christians still discuss what the baptism added: most see it as the public anointing of the Messiah for his ministry and the revelation of the Trinity, rather than a change in who he is.

observe: List the images John uses in verses 7 to 12. What does each picture about the coming one or the coming judgment?
What does John say about himself and about the one coming after him in verses 11 and 14?
What three things happen in verses 16 and 17 as Jesus comes up out of the water?
interpret: Why does John say that having Abraham as father will not protect anyone? What were his hearers relying on?
What might Jesus mean by saying it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness?
How do Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1 together shape the meaning of the Father's words?
apply: What forms of spiritual inheritance or religious background might you be tempted to rely on instead of genuine repentance?
What would fruit in keeping with repentance look like in one specific area of your life right now?
Before Jesus had preached a sermon or done a miracle, the Father said he was well pleased with him. How does that change the way you think about God's love and your own achievements?
